\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]

This analysis extends the main 8-generator LOGO evaluation (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}) to nine generators by adding Gemma-2-2B, a model from a previously unrepresented architecture family (Gemma).

\caption{9-generator LOGO evaluation. Each row holds out the listed generator at test time. 3-class: gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. 95\% bootstrap CIs in brackets.}
\label{tab:9gen-logo}

\begin{tabular}{llr cc cc}
\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\

Pythia-1B       & Pythia  & 1.0B & 0.857 & [0.848, 0.866] & 0.785 & --- \\

Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia  & 2.8B & 0.812 & [0.801, 0.822] & 0.728 & --- \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}

\paragraph{Overall comparison.}
Adding Gemma-2-2B reduces the mean 3-class LOGO F1 from 0.770 (8-gen) to 0.751 (9-gen), a drop of $\Delta = -0.019$.
The per-generator F1 values for the original eight generators shift by at most $[-0.011, +0.002]$, indicating that the inclusion of Gemma data in training does not destabilize existing generalization patterns.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.763 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).

Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).

DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.789, binary F1\,=\,0.830; evaluated on the 5-generator subset for which cross-model chains were available), though these generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The central finding is that recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped: autoregressive sampling with fixed top-$p$ plausibly truncates the conditional distribution at a consistent shape regardless of input, while mean surprisal systematically decreases as the model conditions on its own increasingly typical outputs.
Permutation importance, Granger causality, and feature intervention analyses confirm that DDR features carry causal predictive power beyond correlation: drifting features contribute $5.3\times$ more to classification than near-stationary ones, and 6/7 features exhibit significant Granger causality across generation depths, with entropy\_min as the sole exception (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
This asymmetry is not intrinsic to recursion but parameter-dependent: at $t{=}1.0$, the location signal collapses ($\rho$ from $-0.60$ to $-0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), and semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift (elaboration F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ continuation 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}), consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}; cross-type transfer remains viable (F1\,=\,0.753).

Several boundary conditions constrain practical applicability.
Document-level gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for automated filtering but sufficient for corpus-level flagging ($O(1/\sqrt{n})$ error scaling); the primary difficulty is distinguishing gen-1 from gen-2+, consistent with DDR producing the smallest location shift at the first recursive step (86\% false negatives; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
Cross-temperature transfer degrades when test-time temperature exceeds training ($t{=}0.7 \rightarrow 1.0$: overall 3-class F1 drops from 0.789 to 0.723; the most affected single generator, Qwen3-1.7B, drops to per-generator F1\,=\,0.418; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-temp}); depth fingerprinting assumes matched or lower temperature.
These patterns hold across reference model families (F1 within 0.013; Table~\ref{tab:cross-ref}).

DDR occupies a distinct position among recursive generation phenomena.
Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes irreversible degradation from \emph{retraining} on model outputs; inference-chain drift operates in a different regime where parameters are fixed, drift is fully reversible, and shape features are affected an order of magnitude less.
This divergence has practical implications: model collapse remediation focuses on restoring tail coverage, while inference-chain contamination preserves shape and thus requires location-based detection---a strategy that DDR directly enables.

Levene tests reject strict equal-variance ($p < 10^{-10}$); Glass's $\Delta$ (using gen-1 SD) amplifies drifting effects (entropy mean $\Delta{=}1.41$, hapax $\Delta{=}0.94$) while near-stationary features remain negligible ($\Delta \leq 0.10$), yielding a ${\geq}9.5\times$ gap. Cliff's $\delta$ corroborates the partition (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
Shape-feature CV shift ($<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features) supports ``near-stationary'' as a practical characterization.
Five features fall cleanly into the drifting or near-stationary groups under both $\rho$ and $d$; the remaining two require qualification: entropy min's pooled $|\rho|$ (0.40) reflects change concentrated at the gen-0/gen-1 boundary, but for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ it is near-stationary ($d{=}0.03$), placing it in the near-stationary group; entropy std shows a substantial level shift ($d{=}0.55$) despite low monotonicity ($|\rho|{=}0.16$), making it the sole intermediate feature.
Entropy min exhibits a discrepancy between location-based (Cohen's $d$\,=\,0.016) and rank-based (Cliff's $\delta$\,=\,0.354) effect sizes, indicating distributional shape change without location shift: recursive generation produces more extreme minimum-entropy tokens while preserving the mean. The near-stationary label refers specifically to location stability; rank-order sensitivity is documented in Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}.
The location/shape decomposition rests on the convergence of $\rho$, Levene, CV shift, and $d$, not the omnibus KS statistic alone.
Per-generator TOST equivalence testing confirms the partition is not a pooling artifact; holdout generator validation confirms stability across two 4/4 splits (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
Bootstrap resampling (1{,}000 iterations) confirms these equivalence conclusions are robust: all three near-stationary features achieve 100\% rejection rate, with effect-size CIs well within the $d{=}0.20$ margin (Appendix~\ref{app:tost-bootstrap}).
Tail decay shows generator-dependent variation ($d{=}0.15$--$0.22$), but reclassifying it as intermediate preserves the core split and classification performance.

\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
Permutation importance: hapax ratio (0.35), entropy mean (0.23), TTR (0.18).
PCA confirms the three drifting features share a single latent dimension (92.3\% variance, loadings 0.56--0.59; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}); replacing them with PC1 costs only 1.1\,pp binary F1, and retaining any single drifting feature with the four non-drifting features yields F1\,=\,0.692 (vs.\ 0.701 full).
DDR's contribution is identifying which distributional properties (NLL location vs.\ shape) are depth-sensitive; PC scores achieve equivalent classification but obscure which specific properties drift.

\subsection{TOST Bootstrap Stability}\label{app:tost-bootstrap}

To verify that the equivalence conclusions in \S\ref{app:tost} are not sensitive to sample composition, we assess their stability under bootstrap resampling.
For each of four representative features, we run 1{,}000 bootstrap iterations (base seed\,=\,42): each iteration independently resamples with replacement from the gen-1 and gen-2+ pools, recomputes Cohen's $d$ and the TOST $p$-value (equivalence margin $|d| < 0.20$).

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\footnotesize
\caption{Bootstrap stability of TOST equivalence ($B{=}1{,}000$, margin $|d|{<}0.20$). Rejection rate = fraction of bootstrap iterations where TOST rejects non-equivalence at $\alpha{=}0.05$.}
\label{tab:tost-bootstrap}
\begin{tabular}{l c c c}
\toprule
\textbf{Feature} & \textbf{Rejection rate} & \textbf{Median $d$} & \textbf{$d$ 95\% CI} \\
\midrule
entropy\_max  & 100\% (1000/1000) & 0.062  & [0.037, 0.088] \\
entropy\_min  & 100\% (1000/1000) & $-$0.016 & [$-$0.042, 0.011] \\
tail\_decay   & 100\% (1000/1000) & 0.088  & [0.065, 0.111] \\
\midrule
entropy\_std  & 0\% (0/1000)      & 0.458  & [0.435, 0.479] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All three near-stationary features achieve a 100\% rejection rate across 1{,}000 bootstrap iterations, and their effect-size 95\% CIs fall entirely within the $\pm 0.20$ equivalence margin.
Entropy std, included as an intermediate control, is never rejected (0\%), with its CI $[0.435, 0.479]$ lying entirely outside the margin.
No feature exhibits boundary-crossing---the classification of each feature is unanimous across all bootstrap samples, confirming that the equivalence conclusions are robust to resampling variability.

This analysis extends the 8-generator LOGO evaluation to nine generators by adding Gemma-2-2B, a model from a previously unrepresented architecture family (Gemma).
All results use class-balanced LOGO; the 8-gen averages here (0.770/0.694) differ slightly from Table~\ref{tab:logo-results} (0.762/0.694), which uses an unfiltered protocol.

\centering
\caption{9-generator LOGO evaluation. Each row holds out the listed generator at test time. 3-class: gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+; binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+. 95\% bootstrap CIs in brackets.}
\label{tab:9gen-logo}

\toprule
\textbf{Generator} & \textbf{Family} & \textbf{Params} & \textbf{3-class F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} \\
\midrule

Pythia-2.8B     & Pythia  & 2.8B & 0.812 & [0.801, 0.822] & 0.728 & --- \\
Qwen3-1.7B      & Qwen    & 1.7B & 0.811 & [0.800, 0.823] & 0.746 & --- \\
OLMo-2-1B       & OLMo    & 1.5B & 0.773 & [0.762, 0.784] & 0.692 & --- \\
Llama-3.2-3B    & Llama   & 3.2B & 0.759 & [0.748, 0.770] & 0.680 & --- \\
Qwen3-8B        & Qwen    & 8.2B & 0.696 & [0.683, 0.709] & 0.647 & [0.631, 0.664] \\

Mistral-7B      & Mistral & 7.0B & 0.605 & [0.593, 0.617] & 0.534 & --- \\
\midrule

\textbf{Average (8-gen)} & & & \textbf{0.770} & & \textbf{0.694} & \\
